solution: The chapter defines an international problem as one that "affect[s] many countries and eventually all the countries of the world" and then names its own scope: "we shall therefore study problems related to human rights, environment and terrorism. Even the questions of refugees are now assuming global proportions. Hence we shall consider this issue as well." A refugee section follows (Jews, 1971 East Pakistan, Syria). The other three options — the Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute, Kaveri water sharing and Naxalism in Andhra Pradesh — are all internal to India; the chapter's own 'Let's do it!' exercise asks students to sort such items into national versus international.

The 'Do you know?' box lists what the Declaration contains: "There are 30 articles in the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights ... there are provisions of economic rights like right to work and equal pay for equal work", and it closes by noting that a Declaration of the Rights of the Child was proclaimed on 20th November 1959. So options (a), (c) and (d) are all explicitly present in the chapter; the right to information is nowhere mentioned among the human rights this chapter lists, making it the odd one out in this 'not included' stem.

The 'Secure environment' section says: "At the international level, the awareness and need of saving the environment was expressed in 1970. ... These activists celebrated the first Earth Day on 22nd April 1970" — the chapter's only day observed at the international level, and its projects section asks for a report on Earth Day. Teachers' Day, Children's Day and Flag Day are Indian national observances and are not mentioned anywhere in the chapter.
